newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's EPS prepares to restructure, privatise.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's EPS prepares to restructure, privatise.

text.p: Serbia's power company Elektroprivreda Srbije (EPS) said on Thursday it planned to restructure and privatise but immediately tried to soothe workers' fears of massive lay-offs.

"EPS is one of the key national resources -- it is not for sale but for transformation. EPS wants to become efficient and to attract foreign capital," EPS General Manager Slobodan Babic said at a meeting with the company's trade unions.

Dragan Kostic, president of the EPS Board of Directors, said plans to restructure included ownership transformation, structural adjustment and organisational reform. "Our intention is to make EPS an internationally respectable company."
While the EPS management revealed no details on how the company would restructure and privatise, workers expressed fears they would feel consequences of any reforms.
"We demand a comprehensive EPS restructuring programme. It would not be good to sell a part of the company, collect money and sack workers," EPS trade union head Radovan Perovic said.
Workers feared privatisation in Serbia would spark big social problems like in other transition economies, he said.
EPS trade union had asked to meet management after newspaper reports that the company was about to be sold.

The daily Privredni Pregled, quoting unnamed sources, said EPS privatisation was set for early this autumn and saw Italian and Greek companies becoming strategic partners acquiring 49 percent stake for as much as $1 billion. Other reports also saw German and Czech firms as potential buyers.

"EPS is not for sale. At the moment it is not ready for its ownership transformation. We need a serious EPS restructuring programme, what parts need substantial investment and then we shall decide where to seek capital, via strategic partnerships or markets," Serbian Privatisation Minister Milan Beko said.
"Many foreign companies come, they are interested in EPS.... They constantly talk, but there are no negotiations yet and no decision has been made," he said.
Beko insisted strategic partnerships were good for long-term development.

"Infrastructure demands constant modernisation, managerial upgrading and infusion of capital. We must look for a strategic partner in those areas which are part of world technological integrations. In other cases, we can turn to financial markets," Beko told reporters.

The company's trade union demanded that EPS privatisation must be transparent, that any sale is conducted via public tenders, that it must be socially fair and that the management accepts only fresh capital injections.
Trade unions have initially opposed any idea to privatise the system grouping 23 companies and employing 61,500 workers.

"We have agreed to privatisation after the government, political parties and economists agreed to it. We also agree it must be fast and compulsory but privatisation of infrastructure systems comes last, not first," Perovic said.
Elektroprivreda Srbije is a 100-percent state-owned company for power generation, transmission and distribution.

EPS had asked the Belgrade-based Economics Institute and Deloitte & Touche to assess its capital and prepare a plan for its comprehensive restructuring and privatisation. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 311 4254
